The previous surah has already explained the splitting of the sky. What is added here is that this act will take place in obedience to Allah, and that it is fitting and deserved that it should do so, fulfilling this right of Allah, because it is Allah's right that His commands be obeyed.

"And it has listened to its Lord and it is right that it should do so" (84:2).

It listens to its Lord and obeys Him, and that is its right. Regarding "adhinat" (listened/obeyed): the sense of "idhn" here is either announcement or permission. The meaning is that it will comply with Allah's command to split apart. The meaning of "huqqat" is that this right of Allah has become binding upon it, and it has acknowledged that this is Allah's right over it. This too is a kind of expression of submission and obedience: that this is Allah's established right over the heavens.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 84, verse 3:

﴿وَإِذَا الْأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾ (84:3) "And when the earth is stretched out." This too is a modern scene and concept. What is the meaning of the earth's stretching and its being lengthened? That is, the laws of nature which control this earth and which keep it in its present form will be suspended. That is, they keep it in its present round or oval shape. The manner of expression suggests that this change in the earth will be produced by external factors, because the passive form has been used for it, namely the word "muddat" (was stretched).

The earth will cast out what is within it and become empty (84:4). This is a depiction in which the earth is, as it were, a living, purposeful entity, which is emptying itself by throwing out what is inside it, for there is a great deal within it. For example, there are countless creatures that have been buried within it over the centuries, and the time of their burial is not known, nor is the number of people. Whatever minerals, water and other things lie within the belly of the earth, the knowledge of which belongs to Allah alone, will all come out. For centuries this earth has been carrying these things. When the Hour is established, it will spew out all these things and all these secrets.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 84, verse 5:

"And it will hearken to its Lord and it has the right to do so." The word *idhn* (hearkening, submission) here means obedience to the Lord and carrying out the commands of Allah. Just as this expression was also used for the sky, the meaning is that the earth will be acknowledging that it is Allah's right over it to bow in submission before His commands. The style of expression gives the impression that the earth and the sky are living beings who hear the command of Allah and carry it out by their own will; they respond immediately with "Here I am" and obey in the manner of one who acknowledges and confesses obedience, who believes it is right for him to do so, and so bows in submission, performs this act without compulsion, and without any objection or resistance.

Although on the Day of Resurrection there will be a great upheaval in this universe, and this is one of its scenes, the picture drawn here is dignified and calm. Upon it lie the deep shadows of balance and reverence. The impressions that remain on the screen of feeling are those of obedience, submission, contentment, humility, reverence, and obedience without objection or argument or dispute.

In such an atmosphere, a call comes from the Lord the Exalted. In it, man is addressed by the name of humanity, showing him: look how this whole universe and these heavens and earth have bowed in obedience, and consider obedience to Allah as a right upon themselves.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 84, verse 6:

یایھا الانسان (6:84) "The one whom the Lord, in His mercy, created in such a form, and to whom Allah gave the distinctive quality of humanity over the whole of creation. It is fitting that he should be foremost in recognising his Lord, and more submissive before Allah than this entire universe, the heavens and the earth. Allah breathed into his body of His own spirit, gave him the strength and the understanding so that he could reach his Lord, kindled the lamp of His light within his being, and placed in him a longing to obtain the bounties of Allah, to attain spiritual purity through them, to ascend to boundless heights, and to reach the furthest limits of perfection that a human being can reach. Let it be remembered that the horizons of human progress and perfection are very vast."

یایھا الانسان ................................ فملقیہ (6:84) "O man! You are journeying laboriously towards your Lord and you will meet Him. O man, you are passing your life's journey in this world with great hardship. You are carrying your burden, striving, with your breath heavy. The path is difficult, and having traversed this laborious path, where will you arrive? Your place of return is to your Lord, and the only refuge is the court of God, and you are reaching it after this struggle and hardship.

O man! In this world you are also obtaining the necessities of life with great effort. If someone does not need to perform physical labour, then worry over livelihood and mental anxiety afflict everyone. Both the prosperous and the poor are certainly anxious; both labour, although the nature of the labour differs. Otherwise, toil and struggle are an inseparable part of human life. Yet the capitalist and the destitute both, in the end, arrive before Allah.

O man! On this earth you will never find true comfort. Comfort and ease will be in the Hereafter, but for those who submit with their heads bowed and obey the commands of the Lord, and who earn something for the Hereafter. The toil of this earth is of one kind, though its colours may differ and its flavours be distinct; but when a person reaches the Lord, the difference in outcomes will be real. One group will be in such hardship that the toil of the earth will appear very different and slight by comparison, and the other group will receive such reward that, in comparison with it, all the fatigues of the earth will vanish, so that it will seem as though they never saw any suffering at all. O man! You have been distinguished by being given the quality of humanity. Choose for yourself the end and the station that befits your humanity, that is suitable to the quality Allah has given you. Seek that comfort, that joy and that blessing which are in the Hereafter.

Since this call contained an indication of the end of humanity, it is immediately stated what end humanity will reach, after this laborious struggle, in each of the two outcomes."

Those who are given their record in their right hand, Allah will be pleased with them. They will be fortunate, believing and virtuous, and Allah will be pleased with them and the decision of their salvation will be made. Their reckoning will be carried out with gentleness. The agents of Allah will not question them excessively, nor will they go into the depths of the reckoning. Its portrayal has been made in the Hadith of the Messenger. I think that if these Hadith are read, no further explanation is needed.

It is narrated from Hadrat Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The one whose reckoning is scrutinised will certainly be punished. She says: I said, "Has Allah not said, 'He will be given an easy reckoning' ?" Then he said: "That is not a success from the reckoning; rather, it is only a presentation. On the Day of Resurrection, the matter will be that the one whose reckoning is taken will be punished." (Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi, Nasai)

There is another narration from Hadrat Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her). She says that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a prayer saying: "O Allah, reckon with me with an easy reckoning." When the Messenger (ﷺ) finished the prayer, I asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what is an easy reckoning?" He said: that the book of accounts is looked at and one is pardoned and let go. "Aishah, on that day, the one who is questioned in detail is destroyed." (Ahmad, with the condition of Muslim, from Abdullah ibn Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him)

In sum, his record is given in his right hand, his reckoning will be easy, and he will be saved.

ۥ"And he will return to his people joyfully" (9:84). That is, to those among his people who had already entered Paradise before him. This manner of expression shows that in Paradise too there will be like-minded people, and each person will be among his righteous family and friends. The portrayal of the one who is saved is exactly this: he will be going joyfully toward his companions, friends and family, and he will have the double joy of salvation and of reunion, and then (he will be) in the gardens.

This was the condition of the people of the right hand. In contrast, there is a completely different condition for those who will be seized, for the consequences of their evil deeds. These people will not even want to take their record of deeds.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 84, verses 10–12:

As for the one who is given his record from behind his back, he will cry out for destruction and will enter a blazing Fire. (84:10–12)

Such scenes were depicted earlier in the Qur'an in this manner: the record of those who succeed is given in the right hand, and that of the people of Hell in the left hand. But the picture here is somewhat different. In this image, the people of Hell are being given their record from behind their backs. Therefore there is no contradiction in the picture: it is being given in the left hand, from behind. This is the picture of a person who does not want to take his record; he cannot face it, and he is in severe distress and flight.

The real matter is that we do not know the states of being given the record in the right hand or in the left hand. We only understand that the first group are those who are saved and will enter Paradise, and the others are those who are failed and disappointed and will enter Hell and be destroyed. This is the essential point, not how the condition will be. Yet the form and appearance that the Qur'an has described certainly leave deep effects upon a person, and a person trembles from fear. The reality of these circumstances is known only to Allah, as to how these stages will be passed.

This wretched one, who spent his life on earth in tireless struggle, and reached before Allah exhausted, yet was immersed in disobedience and rebellion, laden with the burden of sins. Now, upon arriving here, he comes to know his end; he meets an evil outcome. Now he knows that an endless hardship has begun, so this wretch now calls out for death, begging for final annihilation so that he may escape the misfortune that is about to befall him. Let it be remembered that a person seeks refuge in the embrace of death only when he understands that there is no other path to salvation, no place of escape. Then death becomes his last wish. The poet al-Mutanabbi captured this meaning in this verse:

Kafa bika da'an an tara al-mawta shafiyan
Wa hasbu al-manaya an yakun amaniyan

"It is a sufficient affliction for you that you regard death as a cure, and it is enough misery that death should become a longing (and not come)."

Therefore, what greater wretchedness could there be, and what greater calamity, than that he "will enter a blazing Fire" (84:12). And this person will now long for death, which will never be fulfilled... Now let us briefly show a glimpse of this person's past, due to which he reached this end.

"Verily, he used to be among his people, joyful." (13:84) He was devoted to the present and was a slave to it, and heedless of the future. He was careless about what awaited him on the Day of Resurrection. He attached no importance to the Hereafter and made no preparation for it.

Indeed, he used to be among his family, joyful. He thought that he would never return. (This was his condition in the world, and that has passed.) Today the Qur'an has brought us to the field of the Resurrection, the world has passed away, and here reckoning is taking place, and the Qur'an's style has rolled up time and place.

Indeed, he thought he would never return. He thought he would not go back to his Lord. Had he believed that he was to go before Allah, he would have prepared for that presentation and given some importance to the Hereafter. But he had no certainty; rather, his assumption was that there is no Resurrection at all.

Indeed, [the man] thought he would never return [to Allah]. Yes, but his Lord was ever watching him. (Qur'an 84:14–15)

Why did he not think that he would return? His Lord was watching his conduct. He supposed that he would never return to Allah, but the reality is that his Lord was fully aware of his circumstances, encompassing his true self, and acquainted with all his undertakings and all his movements. Allah knew what end he would reach and that Allah was to punish him for what he had done. Thus it happened: when, according to Allah's knowledge, he had spent his life in accordance with Jahannam, and this was what he had to do.

In contrast to the picture of this wretched man is the picture of another person who is righteous. Although in his limited worldly life he was happy and cheerful within the circle of his family, his life as a whole was in some way laborious. In comparison, this righteous person now returns joyfully in the Hereafter to his family and dependents. The worldly life was brief and limited, but the life of the Hereafter is long and unbounded. That life is now free of restraint, pleasant, and lasting, and is free of every kind of hardship, anxiety, and fatigue.

Now the readers finish this long and deep journey. In it they have seen countless scenes and taken impressions; now the context takes them into those moments of the universe in which their own lives are being spent. Here people are shown those scenes of the universe in which the human being himself also appears. These things bear witness that the human being and this universe spread around him move according to a profound plan, a most precise measure and destiny, and that the changing moments and circumstances of this world and of man are the result of this profound plan and destiny.

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb on Surah 84 (Al-Inshiqaq), verse 16:

These are several scenes. The Qur'an swears by them and thereby turns the human heart toward them, so that one reflects upon them. In this way the human heart and mind are filled with signs and impressions. These moments of human life have a particular character: on the one hand there is humility and stillness, and on the other hand there is awe-inspiring majesty. Just as the opening of the Surah was with majestic yet quiet scenes, so too are these moments and scenes.

The time of twilight (shafaq) is the time when everything becomes frightened. After sunset, deep silence and shadows of fear fall upon the human soul as well. Human thought bids them farewell, and farewells always carry the shadows of silence and sorrow. Then come the frightening moments of the night, in which there is the terror of darkness. And finally, in the darkness of the night, everything is enveloped and falls silent, and there is an atmosphere of awesome stillness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 84, verse 17:

﴿وَاللَّيْلِ وَمَا وَسَقَ﴾ (84:17) "And by the night and what it gathers together."

The night and what is gathered within it, and the things it takes up. Without naming them, every known and unknown thing that comes under the veil of the night; whatever is gathered in the night, and the things it embraces to its bosom. Among them are all things, all living creatures, all emotions, and all hidden worlds. All the things that move upon the earth, or that flow secretly within the human conscience. In short, the imagination travels far and returns, and human thought and reflection cannot encompass all the scenes that are the signified meaning of this brief phrase of the Qur'an.

﴿وَاللَّيْلِ وَمَا وَسَقَ﴾ (84:17) "By the night and what it gathers together." By it, a state of humility, reverence, and a fearful, awe-inspiring tranquility settles over human consciousness, and this state is in harmony with the state of twilight and the descent of night.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 84, verse 18:

﴿And by the moon when it becomes full,﴾ (84:18). This too is a quiet and enchanting, beautiful scene: the nights in which the moon becomes full and spreads its cool, gentle and thought-provoking light over the earth. What a beautiful sight it is, in silence and a cool atmosphere, both material and apparent, and also spiritual and intellectual. It is a scene and a journey that harmonises with the coming of evening, twilight and night. The basic elements of this scene are beauty and majesty, humility and reverence, silence and tranquillity.

These great cosmic scenes come before us in the form of extremely beautiful, extremely thought-provoking and extremely awe-inspiring rapid glimpses, and they address the human heart and vision, the hearts that do not hear the call of this universe. These scenes are invoked as oaths so that they may have an impact on the human heart and conscience, and so that it may accept their freshness, their beauty, and their signs and effects, and see the hand that has determined their outlines and that brings these scenes and glimpses one after another. In these glimpses there are these scenes, and people also change, and their circumstances also change; but it is a matter of great regret that, despite witnessing these scenes, people remain heedless.

﴿لَتَرْكَبُنَّ طَبَقًا عَنْ طَبَقٍ﴾ (84:19) "You will surely pass from one stage to another." That is, after one situation you will be confronted with another situation, just as Allah has decreed for you. Here the word "riding" (sawari) is used for the change from one state to another. In Arabic it is a common idiom to say that one "rides" difficulties when facing matters, dangers, circumstances and hardships. It is said:

"The one in distress rides upon difficult matters, and he knows how to ride them, that is, how to master them."

The difficulties and trials that the Islamic movement will face will come one after another as successive and extremely severe stages. These circumstances will come in accordance with Allah's decree and will, which guide people along this path, and the hand of divine power carries them to a limit, from which the next stage begins. Just as the twilight appears, then night comes and spreads over everything, and the moon rises and becomes a full moon, so a person will traverse this journey and reach Allah, as was explained in the preceding paragraph. The succession of harmonious paragraphs and phrases, the progression from one meaning and thought to another, and the movement from one scene to the next, are a miraculous and unique feature of the Noble Qur'an that cannot be imitated.

After these scenes, signs, observations and the atmosphere of delightful moments that came one after another throughout this surah, it is astonishing that a sensible person, despite these proofs of faith, does not believe, although in this universe and within their own souls there are abundant and clear proofs.

Indeed, they have no justification for this. In the scenes of this universe and in human souls themselves there are such signs and traces that wherever the human heart turns, they invite it to contemplation, and wherever a living mind is at work, these signs come forward in abundance. These signs and traces are so numerous, so strong and so profound that if a human heart turns towards them even slightly, attentive to them, they surround it. If it lends them an ear, pays attention and listens to what they say, these signs whisper to it everywhere and also speak aloud.

﴿So what is the matter with them that they do not believe, and when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate?﴾ (84:20–21). The Qur'an speaks to them in a natural language, opens their hearts to the signs of nature and the indications of faith found in the horizons and in their own souls, and stirs in their hearts the feelings of God-consciousness (taqwa), obedience, and humility and submissiveness; and this itself is prostration for human hearts.

The truth is that this universe is very beautiful; on every side within it are signs of divine power, and within it there are such manifestations, such lights and such scenes that they fill the human heart with feelings of humility and submissiveness.

Then, this Qur'an too is beautiful and full of indications, and within it too there are such indications, such scenes and such evidences which introduce the human heart to this universe and to the Lord of the universe. And by placing in the human mind and heart the great truths of this great universe, they turn it towards the exalted and supreme Creator of this universe. How magnificent it is!

The real matter is that those who have disbelieved have set themselves upon denial; rejecting the truth has become, as it were, their second nature. Denial is their mark, but the diseases within their hearts, which have led them to make denial their very bed and covering, are another matter. Allah knows them well. This is nothing but mischief, and it is evil intentions that are driving their denial.

Now their speech ends here, and the address turns directly to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 84, verse 24:

So give them the good news of a painful punishment. What an evil good news it is, one that brings no joy, which the one who receives it does not like, and for which no one waits. As for the believers who do not deny, what preparations are made for them? Those who prepare for the Day of Resurrection through righteous deeds are presented as exempt from the fate of those who deny.

In Arabic grammar this is called istithna' munqati' (disjunctive exception). The reason is that the believers were not included at all in the unwelcome and grim "good news" or the black warrant given to the disbelievers. But the purpose of this exceptional manner of expression is to show that those who were excepted are extremely fortunate.

﴿And for them is a reward that never ends﴾: an everlasting reward that will never be cut off and will remain forever. This decisive point is where this surah concludes. It is a short surah, of a few lines, yet it presents broad and thought-provoking themes for reflection.
